summary: A 1971 proposal for NETRJS, a third-level protocol for Remote Job Entry, by R. T. Braden and S. M. Wolfe. Remote job entry lets users submit batch jobs to a distant computer. It was replaced by RFC 189.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 88 describes NETRJS, which lets a remote process submit jobs to the Remote Job Service at CCN. It uses separate network channels to represent an operator console, card reader, printer, and card punch.

questions: how to submit batch jobs over the arpanet
how did netrjs submit remote batch jobs
how many channels did a standard netrjs site use
subtitle: A protocol for remote users to submit batch jobs to a central Remote Job Service.

tldr.problem: Remote users needed a way to access the Remote Job Service at CCN and submit jobs as if using remote batch-terminal devices.
tldr.mechanism: NETRJS simulates operator, card-reader, printer, and punch devices using separate network channels and defines blocks for their data.
tldr.outcome: RFC 88 is an early NETRJS specification and was obsoleted by RFC 189.

today: RFC 88 describes an early NETRJS protocol and was obsoleted by RFC 189.

sections.title: Remote Batch Job Entry
sections.content:
NETRJS is a message protocol and set of control conventions for remote access to the Remote Job Service (RJS) subsystem at CCN. A remote process simulates a batch terminal: it can submit OS/360 jobs through a card-reader stream and receive printed or punched output.

Multiple remote users at one host can act as separate remote sites, identified by terminal IDs of 8 characters. A standard remote site has operator input and output channels plus a card reader, printer, and punch channel.
sections.plainLanguage: A remote process can send batch jobs to CCN and receive their output. Separate channels represent the console and the simulated card reader, printer, and punch.

sections.title: Channels and Data Blocks
sections.content:
NETRJS opens a separate network connection, called a channel, for each simulated device. Card-reader, printer, and punch channels are active only when needed; operator input and output channels stay open through the session.

A network message is a variable-length block of up to 900 bytes. Operator input and output blocks cannot exceed 130 bytes. Blocks include control and device information, and may include a check field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each simulated device has its own channel. Most blocks can be up to 900 bytes, while operator channel blocks are limited to 130 bytes.

sections.title: Starting and Ending a Session
sections.content:
A remote site first requests a connection to the CCN incoming logger, which allocates six consecutive AEN numbers and returns the socket information. The remote site opens the operator input channel and sends a SIGNON command with its terminal ID. If RJS does not recognize the ID or has no available Line Handler for the Network, it closes that channel.

A user can end the session by closing the console input channel or by sending SIGNOFF. With SIGNOFF, RJS waits for current job output to complete before ending the session. If either site terminates the session, the other connections for that remote site should close.
sections.plainLanguage: The remote site requests a session, opens the operator channel, and sends SIGNON with its terminal ID. It can finish by closing the console input channel or sending SIGNOFF.
